file_io.notes: open_and_read teaches open/read/close once; every later topic uses with (context_managers.with_open, owned by context_managers but taught second). Loops over file lines (deferred by B03/B04) are file_io.loop_over_lines. handle_missing_file only applies try/except to files and has pending concept:exceptions (B09 owns try/except itself); if B09 writes its own FileNotFoundError example the stitching pass should make B09's generic try/except topic the prerequisite and keep this file-specific one. encoding='utf-8' (deferred by B03 unicode_encoding) is in encodings_and_binary. Binary images with PIL are B19 lib_pillow. Counting words in a file with a dict (py4e ch. 9) is B07 dictionaries, which can list file_io.loop_over_lines as a prerequisite in a later stitch. `import` lines (csv, json, os, sys) are used as memorised one-liners before B13 modules_imports, as B06 did with `import copy`.

context_managers.notes: with_open is the second file topic and core. write_with_contextlib is non-core (Codecademy only) and pending on concept:generators (yield, B08) and concept:exceptions (try/finally, B09); @contextmanager is used as a memorised line rather than requiring B08 decorators. Class-based context managers (__enter__/__exit__) belong to B11 dunder_methods. Nested managers are file_io.copy_and_transform KP2.

file_paths.notes: Non-core: the browser platform's files sit next to the program, so core file topics use bare names. Terminal-side paths are B01 command_line.absolute_and_relative_paths (a prerequisite). os.path string functions are owned here; filesystem changes (listdir, mkdir, rename, remove) are os_sys_module.

csv_files.notes: Manual split(';') parsing (Helsinki 'Reading CSV files') is file_io.parse_lines_into_data; csv.reader is motivated by its failure on quoted commas. dict_reader_writer has pending concept:dictionaries (B07). pandas read_csv is B18 lib_pandas. Sorting rows by a column needs key=lambda (B08) and was left to that batch's practice.

json_data.notes: json_strings KP1 uses lists only so it works before dicts; KP3-4 and later topics need dicts, hence pending concept:dictionaries. navigate_nested_json is pending concept:nested_data_structures (B07). JSON from HTTP APIs (requests .json()) is B16 apis_http, which should depend on navigate_nested_json. Handling a missing JSON file on first run combines json_data.json_files with file_io.handle_missing_file (practice item for later stitching, not a separate topic).

lib_json.notes: The json module (loads/dumps/load/dump, indent, JSONDecodeError) is fully taught by the json_data topics; a separate topic would duplicate them.

serialization.notes: Only Boot.dev teaches it (in Go, for pub/sub, which is out of scope). One non-core topic that generalises JSON/CSV/text and introduces pickle. Serializing custom objects (to_dict/from_dict) belongs to B11 classes.

os_sys_module.notes: sys.argv is owned by command_line_args; os.path string functions by file_paths; os.environ by B13 environment_variables; subprocess by B13. shutil (copying/removing folder trees) was left out. Uses `import os` / `import sys` before B13 modules_imports as memorised lines.

command_line_args.notes: Non-core because running with arguments needs a terminal (B01 running_scripts.run_from_terminal is non-core); a browser platform would need an 'arguments' box to make these core. *args/**kwargs (which the concept graph places after this) are B08. Validating with try/except int() is B09 practice.

cli_applications.notes: Project-shaped (Boot.dev BookBot, Pokedex REPL): best delivered as multisteps; these two topics teach the reusable structure. Character counting with dicts and sorting the report (BookBot) need B07 dictionaries and B08 key functions and are left as later practice. Command dispatch through a dict of functions is B08 higher_order_functions.

topics.title: Opening a file and reading all of its text
topics.summary: Open a text file by name, read its whole contents into one string with read(), close it, and recognise FileNotFoundError.

knowledge_points.title: open(), read(), close()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# fruits.txt contains three lines: apple, banana, cherry
f = open("fruits.txt")
text = f.read()
f.close()
print(text)
open() gives a file object; read() returns everything in the file as one string.
knowledge_points.practice: Put open/read/close/print lines in order; predict what a short program prints for a given file.

knowledge_points.title: The contents are one string, newlines included
knowledge_points.worked_example:
text = open("fruits.txt").read()
print(len(text.split()))  # 3
print(text.count("\n"))  # 3
Each line ends with \n, so string methods can count words and lines.
knowledge_points.practice: Given a file's contents, predict word, line and character counts computed from read().

knowledge_points.title: read() only gives the text once
knowledge_points.worked_example:
f = open("fruits.txt")
first = f.read()
second = f.read()
print(second == "")  # True
The file object remembers its position; after reading to the end, read() returns "".
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of reading twice; fix a program that reads twice and finds nothing the second time.

knowledge_points.title: A wrong name raises FileNotFoundError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
open("fruit.txt")
# FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'fruit.txt'
The name must match exactly, and Python looks for it in the folder the program runs in.
knowledge_points.practice: Given a folder listing, predict which open() calls succeed and which raise FileNotFoundError.

topics.title: Reading a file line by line
topics.summary: Loop over the lines of a file with for, strip the trailing newline, filter lines, and use readline(), readlines() and splitlines() when they fit.

knowledge_points.title: for line in f gives one line at a time
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("fruits.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line)
# apple, a blank line, banana, a blank line, cherry, a blank line
Each line keeps its \n and print adds another, so output is double-spaced.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of a line loop, including the blank lines; count how many times the loop body runs.

knowledge_points.title: Strip the newline before using a line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("fruits.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        word = line.strip()
        print(word, len(word))  # apple 5 ...
Without strip(), len('apple\n') is 6 and comparisons with 'apple' fail.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a program whose comparison line == 'banana' never matches; predict lengths with and without strip().

knowledge_points.title: Search: only process matching lines
knowledge_points.worked_example:
count = 0
with open("mbox.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        if line.startswith("From:"):
            count += 1
print(count)
The py4e pattern: loop, test each line, act only on the ones you want.
knowledge_points.practice: Write code that counts or prints lines matching a condition (starts with, contains, non-blank).

knowledge_points.title: readline(), readlines() and read().splitlines()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("fruits.txt") as f:
    print(f.readlines())  # ['apple\n', 'banana\n', 'cherry\n']
with open("fruits.txt") as f:
    print(f.read().splitlines())  # ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
readline() reads just the next line; splitlines() gives a list without the newlines.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which call produces a given result; predict the list each call returns for a small file.

topics.title: Turning lines of a file into data
topics.summary: Split each line into fields, convert the numbers, skip a header line, and collect the records into a list for later processing.

knowledge_points.title: Split a line into named fields
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# grades.txt: ana;12;15 then bo;9;7
with open("grades.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        name, a, b = line.strip().split(";")
        print(name, a, b)
Strip first, then split on the separator, then unpack into names.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict fields for lines with different separators; fix a ValueError caused by unpacking into the wrong number of names.

knowledge_points.title: Convert fields and compute per line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("grades.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        name, a, b = line.strip().split(";")
        print(name, int(a) + int(b))  # ana 27, bo 16
Fields are always strings; convert before doing arithmetic.
knowledge_points.practice: Write code that prints a total or average per line; fix a program that prints '1215' instead of 27.

knowledge_points.title: Skip a header line with readline()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("scores.txt") as f:
    header = f.readline()  # 'name;score\n'
    for line in f:
        name, score = line.strip().split(";")
The for loop continues from where readline() stopped, so the header is not parsed.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a program that crashes on int('score'); predict which lines the loop sees after one readline().

knowledge_points.title: Collect records into a list, then process
knowledge_points.worked_example:
records = []
with open("grades.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        name, a, b = line.strip().split(";")
        records.append((name, int(a) + int(b)))
print(records)  # [('ana', 27), ('bo', 16)]
Load once into a list; later code (max, sort, report) works on the list, not the file.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a load function body that returns a list of tuples; then compute a total or best record from it.

topics.title: Writing text to a file
topics.summary: Open a file for writing with 'w', write strings with write(), add the newlines yourself, and write a list of values one per line.

knowledge_points.title: Open with 'w' and call write()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("out.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("hi")
print(open("out.txt").read())  # hi
The second argument 'w' means write; the file is created if it does not exist.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the mode and write call; predict the file contents after a short program.

knowledge_points.title: write() does not add a newline
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("out.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("hi")
    f.write("there")
# out.txt contains: hithere
Unlike print(), write() writes exactly the characters you give it; add "\n" yourself.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict file contents for sequences of write() calls with and without \n; fix a file that came out on one line.

knowledge_points.title: Only strings can be written
knowledge_points.worked_example:
score = 42
with open("score.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write(f"{score}\n")
# f.write(score) raises TypeError: write() argument must be str, not int
Convert numbers with an f-string (or str()) first.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix write() calls that pass numbers; write a formatted line such as 'ana: 12'.

knowledge_points.title: Write a list, one item per line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = ["ana", "bo", "cy"]
with open("names.txt", "w") as f:
    for name in names:
        f.write(name + "\n")
print(open("names.txt").read().splitlines())  # ['ana', 'bo', 'cy']
One write per item, each ending in \n, gives a file that reads back line by line.
knowledge_points.practice: Write code that saves a list of numbers or strings one per line; Parsons for a save-then-reload program.

topics.title: Appending, overwriting and choosing a file mode
topics.summary: Pick between 'r', 'w' and 'a', predict what each does to existing contents, and update a file by reading it, changing the data, and writing it back.

knowledge_points.title: 'a' adds to the end
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("started\n")
Run twice and log.txt has two 'started' lines. Append mode keeps the old contents and writes after them.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict file contents after a program using 'a' is run once, twice, three times.

knowledge_points.title: 'w' wipes the file the moment it opens
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("names.txt", "w") as f:
    pass
print(open("names.txt").read() == "")  # True
Opening with 'w' empties an existing file even if nothing is written. This is the classic way to lose data.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict contents after mixed 'w' and 'a' runs; choose the mode for a high-score file vs a log.

knowledge_points.title: The mode limits what you can do
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("out.txt") as f:
    f.write("x")
# io.UnsupportedOperation: not writable
The default mode is 'r' (read only); a file opened with 'w' or 'a' cannot be read.
knowledge_points.practice: Match each mode to the operations it allows; fix programs that write to a file opened for reading.

knowledge_points.title: Update a file: read, change, write back
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("todo.txt") as f:
    items = f.read().splitlines()
items.remove("buy milk")
with open("todo.txt", "w") as f:
    for item in items:
        f.write(item + "\n")
Read everything first and close; only then reopen with 'w'.
knowledge_points.practice: Parsons for a read-modify-write update; spot the bug where 'w' is opened before the old contents were read.

topics.title: Reading one file and writing another
topics.summary: Process an input file line by line into a new output file, using two files in one with statement and print(..., file=...).

knowledge_points.title: Two with blocks: load, then save
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("names.txt") as f:
    names = f.read().splitlines()
with open("upper.txt", "w") as f:
    for name in names:
        f.write(name.upper() + "\n")
The simplest transform: read everything, close, write the result.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output file for a given input and transformation; fill in the missing write line.

knowledge_points.title: Two files in one with statement
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("names.txt") as src, open("upper.txt", "w") as dst:
    for line in src:
        dst.write(line.upper())
Both files stay open together, so each line can be written as soon as it is read.
knowledge_points.practice: Parsons for a one-with copy program; fix a version that writes to src instead of dst.

knowledge_points.title: print(..., file=f) writes a line for you
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("report.txt", "w") as out:
    print("ana", 27, file=out)
# report.txt contains: ana 27 and a newline
print() converts values, adds spaces and the newline, but sends the text to the file.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite write() calls as print(..., file=...) and predict the resulting file contents.

knowledge_points.title: Filter and reshape records into a new file
knowledge_points.practice: Write a program that converts 'last, first' lines to 'first last' or keeps only qualifying records.

topics.title: Handling a missing file
topics.summary: Apply try/except FileNotFoundError to file programs: report a clear message, fall back to a default, create the file on first run, and re-ask for a file name.

knowledge_points.title: Catch FileNotFoundError with a clear message
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output when the file exists and when it does not; fill in the exception name.

knowledge_points.title: Fall back to a default value
knowledge_points.practice: Write a load function that returns a default when the file is missing; predict best on first and second runs.

knowledge_points.title: Create the file if it does not exist
knowledge_points.worked_example:
try:
    with open("notes.txt") as f:
        notes = f.read().splitlines()
except FileNotFoundError:
    notes = []
    with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
        pass
The except branch can do real work: here it creates an empty file.
knowledge_points.practice: Parsons for a load-or-create helper; fix a version that creates the file with 'w' before trying to read it.

knowledge_points.title: Ask again until the file opens
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the loop for a sequence of typed names; write the loop for a word-count program.

topics.title: Text encodings and binary files
topics.summary: Pass encoding='utf-8' when opening text, recognise UnicodeDecodeError, and read or copy binary files with 'rb' and 'wb'.

knowledge_points.title: Name the encoding when you open text
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("cafe.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read().strip())  # café
Without encoding=, Python uses the computer's default, which differs between systems; utf-8 is the safe choice.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which open() call reads a UTF-8 file correctly on every system; fill in the keyword argument.

knowledge_points.title: A wrong encoding raises UnicodeDecodeError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# cafe.txt was saved as latin-1
with open("cafe.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.read()
# UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xe9 in position 3: invalid continuation byte
The bytes in the file do not match the encoding you asked for.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether reading succeeds for given (saved-as, opened-as) pairs; fix the open() call.

knowledge_points.title: 'rb' gives bytes, not str
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("cafe.txt", "rb") as f:
    data = f.read()
print(data)  # b'caf\xc3\xa9\n'
print(data.decode("utf-8").strip())  # café
Binary mode skips decoding; decode() turns the bytes into text yourself.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the type and length of data read in text vs binary mode.

knowledge_points.title: Copy a binary file with 'rb' and 'wb'
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("photo.jpg", "rb") as src, open("copy.jpg", "wb") as dst:
    dst.write(src.read())
Images, audio and other non-text files must be opened in binary mode on both sides.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a copy that opens an image in text mode; choose the mode for each kind of file.

topics.title: Opening files safely with with
topics.summary: Use with open(...) as f so the file is closed automatically, and know that the file cannot be used after the block ends.

knowledge_points.title: with ... as f: an indented block
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("fruits.txt") as f:
    text = f.read()
print(text)
The file is open inside the indented block and closed automatically when the block ends.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the with line; Parsons for a with-based read-and-print program.

knowledge_points.title: After the block the file is closed
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("fruits.txt") as f:
    pass
print(f.closed)  # True
f.read()
# ValueError: I/O operation on closed file.
The name f still exists, but the file behind it is closed.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether each statement works or raises ValueError; fix code that reads after the block.

knowledge_points.title: Keep the data, not the file
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("fruits.txt") as f:
    lines = f.read().splitlines()
print(len(lines))  # 3
Read what you need into a variable inside the block; use the variable afterwards.
knowledge_points.practice: Restructure programs so all file access happens inside the block and processing happens after it.

knowledge_points.title: Why with beats close()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
f = open("fruits.txt")
text = f.read()
# forgot f.close(): the file stays open until Python cleans up
with closes the file even if you forget, or if an error happens inside the block.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite open/close code using with; choose which programs leave a file open.

topics.title: Writing your own context manager with contextlib
topics.summary: Write a generator-based context manager with @contextmanager whose setup runs before the block and whose cleanup runs after it, even on errors.

knowledge_points.title: Setup, yield, cleanup
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def announce(name):
    print("start", name)
    yield
    print("end", name)

with announce("task"):
    print("working")
# start task / working / end task
Code before yield runs on entry, code after it on exit.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the order of printed lines for several with blocks using a small context manager.

knowledge_points.title: yield a value to bind with as
knowledge_points.worked_example:
@contextmanager
def opened(path):
    f = open(path)
    yield f
    f.close()

with opened("fruits.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
Whatever is yielded becomes the name after as.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the yield; write a context manager that yields a list and prints its length on exit.

knowledge_points.title: try/finally makes cleanup run on errors
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output when the block raises, with and without try/finally; fix a manager that leaks.

topics.title: File paths in your program
topics.summary: Open files in sub-folders with relative paths, know they are relative to the current working directory, use absolute paths, and avoid backslash problems.

knowledge_points.title: A relative path reaches into a folder
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("data/scores.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
'data/scores.txt' means: the folder data, inside the folder the program is running in, then the file.
knowledge_points.practice: Given a folder tree, write the relative path to each file; predict which paths raise FileNotFoundError.

knowledge_points.title: Relative to the working directory, not the script
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import os
print(os.getcwd())  # the folder you ran python from
Running python project/app.py from your home folder makes 'data.txt' mean ~/data.txt, not project/data.txt.
knowledge_points.practice: Given a working directory and a command, predict which file a relative path refers to.

knowledge_points.title: Absolute paths and ..
knowledge_points.worked_example:
open("/Users/ana/notes/todo.txt")  # absolute: same file from anywhere
open("../shared/todo.txt")  # one folder up, then into shared
Absolute paths do not depend on where you run, but break on another computer.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify paths as absolute or relative; resolve .. paths against a given working directory.

knowledge_points.title: Windows backslashes: use / or a raw string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
path = "C:
ew	able.txt"   # 
 and 	 become newline and tab!
path = r"C:
ew	able.txt"  # raw string: backslashes kept
path = "C:/new/table.txt"   # forward slashes also work on Windows
knowledge_points.practice: Spot the broken path among several; fix it two ways.

topics.title: Building and splitting paths with os.path
topics.summary: Join path pieces with os.path.join, take paths apart with basename, dirname and splitext, and check that a path exists before opening it.

knowledge_points.title: os.path.join builds a path
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import os
path = os.path.join("data", "scores.csv")
print(path)  # data/scores.csv (data\scores.csv on Windows)
join uses the right separator for the system, so you never glue '/' by hand.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict joined paths; rewrite string concatenation of paths with os.path.join.

knowledge_points.title: basename and dirname
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(os.path.basename("data/photo.jpg"))  # photo.jpg
print(os.path.dirname("data/photo.jpg"))   # data
basename is the last part; dirname is everything before it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict basename and dirname for several paths, including one with no folder.

knowledge_points.title: splitext separates the extension
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name, ext = os.path.splitext("photo.JPG")
print(name, ext.lower())  # photo .jpg
splitext returns a pair; compare extensions in lower case (CS50 P-Shirt checks input and output match).
knowledge_points.practice: Write a check that two file names have the same extension; predict splitext on names with several dots.

knowledge_points.title: os.path.exists before opening
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output for a given folder listing; write a check that picks a default file when one is missing.

topics.title: Paths as objects with pathlib
topics.summary: Use pathlib.Path to build paths with /, read their parts, check existence, read and write whole files, and list matching files with glob.

knowledge_points.title: Path and the / operator
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("data") / "photo.jpg"
print(p)  # data/photo.jpg
/ joins path parts, like os.path.join but shorter.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed path for several / expressions; translate os.path.join calls to Path.

knowledge_points.title: name, stem, suffix, parent
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(p.name, p.stem, p.suffix, p.parent)
# photo.jpg photo .jpg data
These attributes replace basename, splitext and dirname.
knowledge_points.practice: Match each attribute to its value for given paths.

knowledge_points.title: read_text and write_text
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Path("note.txt").write_text("hi\n")
print(Path("note.txt").read_text().splitlines())  # ['hi']
One call opens, reads or writes, and closes; write_text overwrites like 'w'.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a with-open read as read_text(); predict contents after write_text calls.

knowledge_points.title: List files with glob
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for p in Path(".").glob("*.csv"):
    print(p.name)
# out.csv, people.csv, scores.csv (order not guaranteed)
* matches any characters; sort the names if order matters.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which files a pattern matches in a given folder; write a loop that counts .txt files.

topics.title: Managing files and folders with os
topics.summary: List a folder with os.listdir, make folders with os.makedirs, and rename and delete files with os.rename and os.remove, predicting the errors each can raise.

knowledge_points.title: os.listdir lists a folder
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import os
for name in sorted(os.listdir(".")):
    print(name)
listdir returns a list of names (files and folders, no paths, in no particular order).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of listdir plus filtering by extension; write code counting .txt files in a folder.

knowledge_points.title: Make folders: mkdir vs makedirs(exist_ok=True)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
os.makedirs("backup", exist_ok=True)
os.mkdir("backup")
# FileExistsError: [Errno 17] File exists: 'backup'
exist_ok=True makes creation safe to repeat.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls fail when a folder already exists; fix a script that crashes on its second run.

knowledge_points.title: Rename or move with os.rename
knowledge_points.worked_example:
os.rename("note.txt", "backup/note.txt")
print(os.listdir("backup"))  # ['note.txt']
rename changes a file's path, which also moves it between folders.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict folder contents after a sequence of renames; write the call to move a file into a folder.

knowledge_points.title: Delete with os.remove (no undo)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
os.remove("backup/note.txt")
os.remove("backup/note.txt")
# FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'backup/note.txt'
Deleted files skip the trash; check with os.path.exists first if unsure.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outcomes of remove calls; add an exists check to a cleanup script.

topics.title: Stopping a program with sys.exit and reporting errors
topics.summary: End a program early with sys.exit, pass a message or exit code, and send error messages to sys.stderr.

knowledge_points.title: sys.exit stops the program now
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import sys
print("one")
sys.exit()
print("two")  # never runs
Nothing after sys.exit() runs, wherever it is called from.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of programs that exit inside an if or a loop.

knowledge_points.title: Exit with a message
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the sys.exit call for a failure case; predict what the terminal shows.

knowledge_points.title: Exit codes: 0 means success
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python greet.py
Usage: python greet.py NAME
$ echo $?
1
sys.exit() or reaching the end gives 0; sys.exit('msg') or sys.exit(1) signals failure to the shell.
knowledge_points.practice: Give the exit code for each ending of a program.

knowledge_points.title: Errors go to sys.stderr
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("result: 42")
print("warning: bad line skipped", file=sys.stderr)
stdout is for results, stderr for problems, so redirecting results to a file still shows errors on screen.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify messages as stdout or stderr; rewrite error prints to use file=sys.stderr.

topics.title: Reading command-line arguments with sys.argv
topics.summary: Read the words typed after the script name from sys.argv, convert them to numbers, and loop over sys.argv[1:].

knowledge_points.title: sys.argv is a list of what was typed
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# args.py
import sys
print(sys.argv)
$ python args.py hello 3
['args.py', 'hello', '3']
Index 0 is the script name; the arguments start at index 1.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict sys.argv and len(sys.argv) for several command lines.

knowledge_points.title: Arguments are always strings
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# add.py
import sys
print(sys.argv[1] + sys.argv[2])
print(int(sys.argv[1]) + int(sys.argv[2]))
$ python add.py 2 3
23
5
knowledge_points.practice: Fix programs that join instead of add; predict output with and without int().

knowledge_points.title: Quotes keep spaces together
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python args.py New York
['args.py', 'New', 'York']
$ python args.py "New York"
['args.py', 'New York']
The shell splits on spaces unless the words are quoted.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict sys.argv for command lines with and without quotes.

knowledge_points.title: Loop over sys.argv[1:]
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for name in sys.argv[1:]:
    print(f"hello, {name}")
$ python hi.py ana bo
hello, ana
hello, bo
Slicing off index 0 leaves just the user's arguments.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a script that sums all numeric arguments; fix one that greets the script name.

topics.title: Checking command-line arguments
topics.summary: Check how many arguments were given and whether they are valid, and exit with a usage message instead of crashing.

knowledge_points.title: A missing argument raises IndexError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python greet.py
print(sys.argv[1])
# IndexError: list index out of range
With no arguments sys.argv is just ['greet.py'], so index 1 does not exist.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which command lines crash a given script.

knowledge_points.title: Check len(sys.argv) and print usage
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import sys
if len(sys.argv) != 2:
    sys.exit("Usage: python greet.py NAME")
print(f"Hello, {sys.argv[1]}")
Check before you index; the usage line tells the user how to call the script.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the length check for scripts expecting 1, 2 or 'at least 1' arguments.

knowledge_points.title: Too few vs too many
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the message for several command lines; fix an off-by-one that counts the script name wrongly.

knowledge_points.title: Validate the value, not just the count
knowledge_points.practice: Write validation for a script that expects a .csv file name and a positive number.

topics.title: Command-line options with argparse
topics.summary: Declare positional arguments, typed options with defaults, and on/off flags with argparse, and read them from the parsed args.

knowledge_points.title: A positional argument
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import argparse
parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("word")
args = parser.parse_args()
print(args.word)
$ python ap.py hi
hi
Each add_argument becomes an attribute of args.
knowledge_points.practice: Parsons for a minimal argparse script; predict args values for given command lines.

knowledge_points.title: Options with type and default
knowledge_points.worked_example:
parser.add_argument("-n", "--times", type=int, default=1)
$ python ap.py hi -n 3
hihihi
type=int converts for you; default is used when the option is left out.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict args.times for several command lines; fill in type= and default=.

knowledge_points.title: On/off flags with store_true
knowledge_points.worked_example:
parser.add_argument("--upper", action="store_true")
$ python ap.py hi --upper
HI
A flag takes no value: present means True, absent means False.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict args.upper for command lines with and without the flag; add a --verbose flag.

knowledge_points.title: Free help and error messages
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python ap.py
usage: ap.py [-h] [-n TIMES] [--upper] word
ap.py: error: the following arguments are required: word
argparse checks counts and types itself and prints usage; -h shows help.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether a command line runs or which error argparse prints; compare with the hand-written sys.argv checks.

topics.title: Building a command-line report tool
topics.summary: Assemble a small CLI program (like Boot.dev's BookBot): take a file path from the command line, load and analyse the file in helper functions, and print a formatted report or a clear error.

knowledge_points.title: The shape: arguments, load, analyse, report
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def main():
    path = get_path()
    text = load(path)
    counts = analyse(text)
    report(counts)
main()
Each step is one helper; main() reads like the program's outline.
knowledge_points.practice: Parsons for a main() that wires four helpers in order; match each helper to its job.

knowledge_points.title: Helpers return data; only report() prints
knowledge_points.practice: Fix helpers that print instead of return; write analyse() for a word or line count.

knowledge_points.title: Get and check the path in one helper
knowledge_points.practice: Write get_path() for a tool that also accepts an optional second argument.

knowledge_points.title: A readable report
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def report(path, words):
    print(f"--- Report for {path} ---")
    print(f"{words} words found")
    print("--- End ---")
A fixed header and footer make output easy to read and to check by tests.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the full output of the tool for a given input file; extend report() with a line count.

topics.title: An interactive command loop
topics.summary: Write a program that repeatedly reads a command, dispatches it to a function, handles arguments, quit and unknown commands.

knowledge_points.title: Read commands until quit
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the loop for a sequence of typed commands; predict how many prompts appear.

knowledge_points.title: Dispatch each command through a table of functions
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the dispatch lines of a command loop; fix a loop that calls commands[cmd] without checking the command exists.

knowledge_points.title: Commands with arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = input("> ").split()
command = words[0]
args = words[1:]
# 'add milk eggs' -> command 'add', args ['milk', 'eggs']
The first word picks the action; the rest are its arguments.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict command and args for several inputs; write the add command that appends all args to a list.

knowledge_points.title: Empty input should not crash
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = input("> ").split()
if words:
    run(words[0], words[1:])
Pressing Enter gives [], and words[0] would raise IndexError; only dispatch when there is a word.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a command loop that crashes on an empty line; predict the behaviour for blank and whitespace-only input.

topics.title: Reading CSV files with csv.reader
topics.summary: Read comma-separated files with the csv module, skip the header with next(), and convert fields, instead of splitting on commas by hand.

knowledge_points.title: Why split(',') is not enough
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# people.csv line: "Potter, Harry",London
print(line.strip().split(","))
# ['"Potter', ' Harry"', 'London']
CSV allows quoted fields that contain commas; a hand-written split breaks them apart.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict split(',') results for lines with and without quoted commas; choose when csv is needed.

knowledge_points.title: csv.reader gives a list per row
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import csv
with open("people.csv") as f:
    for row in csv.reader(f):
        print(row)
# ['name', 'city']
# ['Potter, Harry', 'London']
The reader handles quoting; each row is a list of strings.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict rows for small CSV files, including quoted fields and empty fields.

knowledge_points.title: Skip the header with next()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("scores.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    header = next(reader)
    for row in reader:
        print(row)
print(header)  # ['name', 'score']
next() takes one row off the reader; the loop continues with the rest.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a program that crashes on int('score'); fill in the line that saves the header.

knowledge_points.title: Unpack and convert each row
knowledge_points.worked_example:
total = 0
with open("scores.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    next(reader)
    for name, score in reader:
        total += int(score)
print(total)  # 21
Values are still strings; csv does not convert numbers.
knowledge_points.practice: Write code that totals, averages or filters a numeric column; use delimiter=';' for a semicolon file.

topics.title: Writing CSV files with csv.writer
topics.summary: Write rows to a CSV file with writerow and writerows, open it with newline='', and let the writer quote fields that contain commas.

knowledge_points.title: writerow writes one list as one line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("out.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["name", "score"])
    w.writerow(["ana", 12])
# out.csv: name,score / ana,12
Numbers are converted to text for you.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the file contents for a sequence of writerow calls.

knowledge_points.title: Commas inside a field get quoted
knowledge_points.worked_example:
w.writerow(["Potter, Harry", 7])
# written as: "Potter, Harry",7
The writer adds quotes so a reader gets the field back in one piece.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the written line for fields containing commas or quotes.

knowledge_points.title: writerows writes a whole list of rows
knowledge_points.worked_example:
rows = [["bo", 9], ["cy", 14]]
w.writerows(rows)
# two lines: bo,9 and cy,14
Pass a list of lists (or tuples) to write everything at once.
knowledge_points.practice: Write code that saves a list of records (with a header) to CSV.

knowledge_points.title: Always open with newline=""
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("out.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    ...
Without newline="" CSV files written on Windows get an extra blank line after every row.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix the open() call for a CSV writer; choose which of several open calls is correct.

topics.title: CSV rows as dictionaries: DictReader and DictWriter
topics.summary: Read rows as dictionaries keyed by the header with DictReader, and write dictionaries with DictWriter, fieldnames and writeheader.

knowledge_points.title: DictReader uses the header as keys
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("scores.csv") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["name"], int(row["score"]) * 2)
# ana 24
# bo 18
No next() needed: the first line becomes the keys of every row.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict printed values for a DictReader loop; fill in the column name to read.

knowledge_points.title: Values are still strings
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(row)  # {'name': 'bo', 'score': '9'}
DictReader only names the fields; convert numbers yourself before comparing or adding.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a program that sorts or compares scores as text; predict '9' > '12'.

knowledge_points.title: DictWriter: fieldnames and writeheader
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("out.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["name", "score"])
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerow({"name": "ana", "score": 12})
# out.csv: name,score / ana,12
fieldnames fixes the column order.
knowledge_points.practice: Parsons for a DictWriter program; predict the file when the field order changes.

knowledge_points.title: Keys must match the fieldnames
knowledge_points.worked_example:
w.writerow({"name": "ana", "age": 12})
# ValueError: dict contains fields not in fieldnames: 'age'
Every key you write must be one of the fieldnames.
knowledge_points.practice: Spot and fix rows whose keys do not match the fieldnames.

topics.title: JSON text and Python values: loads and dumps
topics.summary: Recognise JSON syntax, turn JSON text into Python lists and dicts with json.loads, and turn Python values into JSON text with json.dumps.

knowledge_points.title: json.loads turns text into Python values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import json
data = json.loads('[1, 2, "a", true, null]')
print(data)  # [1, 2, 'a', True, None]
print(data[2])  # a
The result is a real list you can index, not a string.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the Python value and its type for short JSON texts.

knowledge_points.title: JSON spelling vs Python spelling
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(json.dumps([1, "a", True, None]))  # [1, "a", true, null]
JSON writes true, false and null, and always uses double quotes.
knowledge_points.practice: Translate values between Python and JSON spelling; spot invalid JSON (single quotes, True).

knowledge_points.title: JSON objects become dictionaries
knowledge_points.worked_example:
person = json.loads('{"name": "ana", "age": 31}')
print(person["age"])  # 31
print(json.dumps(person))  # {"name": "ana", "age": 31}
{...} in JSON is an object; Python reads it as a dict.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict lookups on loaded objects; write the dumps call for a given dict.

knowledge_points.title: dumps gives a string; indent makes it readable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
text = json.dumps({"name": "ana", "tags": ["x", "y"]}, indent=2)
print(type(text).__name__)  # str
indent= spreads the text over lines; the data is the same.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the type of loads/dumps results; predict the indented layout of a small value.

topics.title: Saving and loading JSON files
topics.summary: Save Python data to a file with json.dump, load it back with json.load, and update a JSON file by loading, changing and dumping it.

knowledge_points.title: json.dump writes data to a file
knowledge_points.worked_example:
data = {"name": "ana", "scores": [12, 15]}
with open("data.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=4)
dump (no s) writes to a file object; dumps returns a string.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in dump vs dumps; predict the file contents for a small value.

knowledge_points.title: json.load reads it back
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("data.json") as f:
    data = json.load(f)
print(data["scores"][1])  # 15
The loaded value has the same structure that was saved.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values read from a given JSON file; fix code that calls loads on a file object.

knowledge_points.title: Update: load, change, dump
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("data.json") as f:
    data = json.load(f)
data["scores"].append(9)
with open("data.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=4)
The 100 Days password-manager pattern: never edit JSON text by hand in code.
knowledge_points.practice: Parsons for a load-change-save program; predict the saved data after two runs.

topics.title: Digging into nested JSON data
topics.summary: Apply nested-data paths to JSON text from files and web APIs: parse it, collect the fields you need, handle JSON null, and explore an unfamiliar response level by level.

knowledge_points.title: Parse, then follow the path
knowledge_points.worked_example:
data = json.loads('{"results": [{"name": "Oslo", "rating": null}, {"name": "Bergen", "rating": 4.5}]}')
print(data["results"][1]["name"])  # Bergen
Once loaded, JSON is ordinary nested dicts and lists, so the paths from navigate_deep_data apply unchanged.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the lookup expression that reaches a given value in loaded JSON; predict the value of a given chain.

knowledge_points.title: Collect fields into a new list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = []
for place in data["results"]:
    names.append(place["name"])
print(names)  # ['Oslo', 'Bergen']
Most API answers hold a list of similar objects; extract just what you need before processing further (data as in KP1).
knowledge_points.practice: Write code that extracts a list of values meeting a condition (py4e GeoJSON / comment counts).

knowledge_points.title: JSON null arrives as None
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the Python values of JSON fields containing null, true and false; fix a total that crashes on a null field.

knowledge_points.title: Explore an unfamiliar response one level at a time
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(list(data))                         # ['results']
print(type(data["results"]), len(data["results"]))  # <class 'list'> 2
print(list(data["results"][0]))          # ['name', 'rating']
Before writing a path into a big response, print the keys and types of each level; when a path fails, inspect the level above it.
knowledge_points.practice: Given printed keys and types of a response, write the path to a described value; choose what to print next to find a field.

topics.notes: Reconciliation: KP1, KP2 and KP4 duplicated nested_data_structures.navigate_deep_data (paths, looping over the list, KeyError/TypeError per step); rewritten as JSON-specific steps that build on it. Snippets run with Python 3.13.

topics.title: What JSON cannot hold
topics.summary: Predict what changes in a JSON round trip (tuples become lists, keys become strings), which values cannot be saved, and the errors raised by invalid JSON text.

knowledge_points.title: Tuples come back as lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(json.loads(json.dumps((1, 2))))  # [1, 2]
JSON has only arrays, so a tuple is saved as an array and loaded as a list.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the loaded value and type for tuples and nested tuples.

knowledge_points.title: Keys always become strings
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(json.loads(json.dumps({1: "a"})))  # {'1': 'a'}
JSON object keys are text, so data[1] fails after loading; use data['1'] or convert.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict lookups after a round trip; fix code that looks up an int key in loaded JSON.

knowledge_points.title: Some values cannot be saved
knowledge_points.worked_example:
json.dumps({(1, 2): "a"})
# TypeError: keys must be str, int, float, bool or None, not tuple
Only dict, list, str, int, float, bool and None (and tuples, as lists) can be saved, and keys must be simple values; convert anything else first.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify values and dicts as JSON-saveable or not; fix code that saves an unsaveable value or key by converting it first.

knowledge_points.title: Invalid JSON raises JSONDecodeError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
json.loads("{'a': 1}")
# json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)
Single quotes, trailing commas and True/None are Python, not JSON.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the error in each invalid JSON text and fix it.

topics.title: Serialization: saving data and getting it back
topics.summary: Explain serialization as turning in-memory data into text or bytes and back, check that a round trip preserves the data, and choose between plain text, CSV, JSON and pickle.

knowledge_points.title: Serialize and deserialize by hand
knowledge_points.worked_example:
score = 42
text = str(score)        # serialize
print(int(text) == score)  # True: deserialized back
Any save format is a pair of conversions: value -> text/bytes and text/bytes -> value.
knowledge_points.practice: Name the serialize and deserialize steps in short save/load programs.

knowledge_points.title: Test the round trip
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether round trips through text, CSV and JSON give back equal data.

knowledge_points.title: pickle: Python-only bytes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import pickle
b = pickle.dumps({"a": (1, 2)})
print(type(b).__name__, pickle.loads(b))  # bytes {'a': (1, 2)}
pickle keeps Python types exactly, but only Python can read it, and loading untrusted pickle data can run code.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose when pickle is acceptable; predict the type returned by dumps and loads.

knowledge_points.title: Choose a format
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Table of rows for a spreadsheet -> CSV
Nested data for a web API or config -> JSON
Python objects cached by your own program -> pickle
One number or a word list -> plain text
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the best format for each scenario and justify it in one phrase.
